catalog_quote: Like Phom, Wancho is a tone language and, as with Phom, it is convenient to describe the phonology in terms of its syllables and their parts: 1. Initial consonants, 2. Vowels, 3. Final consonants, 4. Tones. ... Unstopped monosyllables (i.e., open syllables and syllables closed with /-m -n -ŋ/) can have one of three contrasting tones; monosyllables ending in /-p -t -k/ can take either of two tones; syllables ending in /-ʔ/ show no tonal contrasts at all. ... The most important fact about the disyllabic tone sequences is that no more than one syllable can have either tone /⁵²/ or tone /¹¹/. In other words, at least one syllable must have tone /⁴⁴/, and many two-syllable words have /⁴⁴/ on both syllables. This means that the tone sequences of two-syllable words are limited to /44-44, 44-52, 44-11, 52-44/, and /11-44/. ... A two-syllable word will then never need more than a single tone mar…

tone_statements.quote: Burling (1999) also provides a description of Wancho phonology and tone system, which he describes as having three tones with no distinction made between checked and open syllables. … He does point out that glottal stop codas are distinct from /p t k/ codas, with no tonal distinction occurring whatsoever with the former. However, for the latter he distinguishes between 44: and 52: contours, as does my consultant Mr. Banwang Losu. … If a claim of tonal correspondences is justified, it would be that Burling’s 44: corresponds to Tangsa-Nocte first tone, 52: to second tone and 11: to third tone.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 297-298, Appendix B 'An Overview of Wancho Tone Categories' (run-up to and start of B.5 Tone Correspondences)
tone_statements.summary: Three tones, following Burling: 44 level, 52 falling, 11 low; own work with one Longding speaker confirms a three-way pitch contrast and 44 vs 52 on stop-final syllables; word categories unsettled.

sources.quote: 'Wancho is a tonal language, with four tones based on phonation distinctions in proto Patkaian (van Dam, 2025).' States the only two published sources of reliable lexical data are Burling & Wangsu (1998) and Losu & Morey (2023); its bibliography also lists Losu 2021 (MA thesis, Deccan College) and Das Gupta 1979 (Resarun). Silent on stress; used here for bibliography, confirms tonal status.

sources.citation: Losu, Banwang & Stephen Morey. 2023. The Wancho language of Kamhua Noknu village. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 46(2): 201-234. doi:10.1075/ltba.00014.los (CC BY 4.0 author manuscript, La Trobe OPAL item 29044691).
sources.quote: 'Wancho has three tones on open syllables (vowel and nasals final)' with a minimal triplet nga1 'tired' (low) / nga2 'to become mad' (mid) / nga3 'mithun' (high); Praat F0 values 100-80, 100-100, 110-110 Hz, approximate Chao 31, 33, 44: 'We can classify Tone 1 as low mid-low falling, Tone 2 as mid level and Tone 3 as high level.' Verb stem alternation is 'mostly expressed by tone variation between the stems' ('speak' ngau1 vs 'language' ngau3). Also notes reduction of first syllables to 'a toneless prefix /kə-/' (sesquisyllables), 'not observed by Burling and Mankai (1998)'. No word-stress rul
sources.locator: Sec. 2.3 'Tones' and 2.3.1 'A note on stem alternation', AAM pp.13-14; sesquisyllable/toneless-prefix remarks AAM p.12
sources.note: Only post-1998 published phonological description (Upper Wancho variety, instrumental F0 for the three tones); adds a second dialect and a second, independent source to a record that rests on one 1998 article. downloaded now; confirms tonal, no stress rule.

sources.citation: Everson, Michael. 2017. Proposal to encode the Wancho script in the UCS. ISO/IEC JTC1/SC2/WG2 N4787R2 = L2/17-067R2, 2017-10-22 (tone analysis credited to Banwang Losu and Stephen Morey).
sources.quote: 'Tones are marked in various ways in different varieties of Wancho ... in an Upper Wancho dialect, it is the low tone which is the most common tone, but in a Lower Wancho dialect, it is the high tone which is the most common ... Syllables checked with the glottal stop are neutral as to tone.' Lists Upper Wancho tones as low, mid, high, checked and Lower Wancho as high 44, falling 52, low 11, checked (the latter explicitly from Burling & Wangsu 1998). No mention of stress.

tone.summary: Group-level only: most Patkaian varieties lexically tonal with 3-5 tones (4 most common in the Northern branch: three from phonation + one checked); nothing stated for Konyak specifically.

sources.note: Comparative reconstruction of Proto-Northern-Naga phonology and basic lexicon; the UMI abstract (read in the Glottolog record) lists the reconstructed distinctions as consonantal prefixes, manner series of initial stops, initial clusters, four position classes of initial nasals and vowel length in open and closed syllables; tone is not mentioned in the abstract, and the Wancho sources available in 1983 were not tone-marked, so any tone treatment is unverified. Glottolog types it overview;comparative;phonology.
